papers.title: Chemistry by Design (CbyD): A Machine-Readable Dataset of Expert-Curated Total Synthesis Routes
papers.abstract: Chemistry by Design (CbyD) is an open-access educational database of published total syntheses launched in 2011. It was designed to help students and practitioners learn organic reactions and synthetic strategies by depicting every step of published natural product and drug syntheses. Motivated by advances in machine learning for organic synthesis and by requests from academic and industrial researchers, we present a machine-readable version of CbyD for use in cheminformatics and computer-aided synthesis planning (CASP). The released dataset (v2026.11) contains 3,502 routes comprising 56,640 reactions toward 2,902 unique targets. Compared with patent-derived datasets, CbyD reactions are more complex, more frequently change stereochemistry, and are less likely to be covered by patent-derived reaction templates, and CbyD routes are longer and more convergent than those in commonly used CASP benchmarks. We also analyze how molecular complexity changes along these routes and identify transformations associated with large complexity increases. The CbyD dataset will be expanded through versioned public releases that incorporate new routes and community-contributed corrections.

papers.title: Recursive extrema extraction tracks temporal organization through progressive data reduction
papers.abstract: Temporal organization is commonly characterized at a prescribed observational scale. Here, a sequence is repeatedly reduced by retaining only the local maxima surviving the preceding extraction. After each step, retained maxima are re-indexed, discarding the original clock and generating a hierarchy whose successive scales are determined by the surviving observations. Mean and variance of gaps between local maxima define hierarchical maxima-gap statistics (HMGS), represented as a trajectory in a two-dimensional statistical plane. Continuous independent and identically distributed (IID) signals generate a distribution-independent reference trajectory, whereas the displacement of structured processes may collapse, persist or amplify relative to it. Crucially, collapse becomes visible only when the accessible hierarchy reaches the characteristic scale of the organization, coupling the required record length to the scale being tested. These fates occur across stochastic, chaotic and event-derived systems and cannot generally be inferred from the first level. HMGS complements analyses based on correlations, entropy, recurrence or prescribed scales by asking a distinct question: whether organization identified at one level remains detectable as the observations themselves define successively deeper levels, without fitting a generative model or prescribing an external coarse-graining scale. In synthetic neuronal populations, superposition creates non-IID trajectories, while source organization persists or is attenuated according to its temporal structure. For mouse population spike trains, median covariance-normalized separation from matched shuffled-source controls decreased from 9.1 times intrinsic null variability at the initial level to 1.2 times after three recursive reductions. HMGS thereby probes which signatures of temporal organization survive progressive data reduction.
